title: Why Don't Cruise Ships Tip Over?
description:
The biggest cruise ships rise more than sixty metres above the water, as tall as a twenty storey building. Yet below the water, the hull goes down only about nine metres. It looks impossible. A tall, thin tower floating on a shallow base should simply fall over in the first strong wind. It does not. Today, ten parts of a cruise ship, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:02 1. The heavy bottom
2:15 2. The wide hull
3:23 3. The stabiliser fins
4:26 4. The anti-heeling tanks
5:33 5. The watertight doors
6:41 6. The pods
7:53 7. The double engine rooms
9:04 8. The orange lifeboats
10:13 9. The inclining test
11:14 10. The lean in turns
12:21 The verdict

Sources:
- Ship stability, centre of gravity, metacentric height: Wikipedia, "Ship stability" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_stability and "Metacentric height" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacentric_height
- Oasis-class dimensions: Wikipedia, "Oasis-class cruise ship" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oasis-class_cruise_ship
- Stabiliser fins: Wikipedia, "Stabilizer (ship)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stabilizer_(ship)
- Anti-heeling and ballast tanks: Wikipedia, "Ballast tank" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballast_tank
- Watertight compartments, Titanic and SOLAS: Wikipedia, "Compartment (ship)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compartment_(ship) and "SOLAS Convention" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOLAS_Convention
- Azipods: Wikipedia, "Azipod" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azipod
- Safe Return to Port (SOLAS, ships built from 2010): IMO https://www.imo.org/
- Lifeboats and international orange: Wikipedia, "Lifeboat (shipboard)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifeboat_(shipboard) and "International orange" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_orange
- Inclining experiment: Wikipedia, "Inclining test" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclining_test
